failure_modes.description: Local cost functions cannot be defined that reliably correlate with network-level performance due to complex traffic dynamics and emergent behaviors.
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic flow exhibits non-linear, chaotic properties where local optimizations often lead to Braess's paradox outcomes where improving individual components degrades overall system performance.

failure_modes.description: Gradient descent mechanisms are fundamentally inadequate for traffic signal optimization because they lack the foresight needed to anticipate future traffic patterns and cannot handle the combinatorial complexity of network-wide optimization.
failure_modes.evidence: Existing research consistently shows that traffic optimization requires global optimization techniques or centralized coordination, not purely local gradient-based approaches, as demonstrated by the failure of similar approaches in real-world implementations.

failure_modes.description: The assumption that the system can escape local minima is unsupported and unrealistic given the complex, high-dimensional optimization landscape of urban traffic networks.
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic signal timing optimization has an enormous solution space with countless local minima, and gradient descent methods without specialized escape mechanisms (like simulated annealing or genetic algorithms) are mathematically guaranteed to get trapped.

failure_modes.description: This approach is not novel as numerous reinforcement learning and adaptive traffic control systems have been implemented with similar mechanisms and have consistently failed to outperform well-engineered fixed-time systems in most real-world scenarios.
failure_modes.evidence: The TRANSYT and SCATS systems from the 1970s-80s already implemented similar optimization concepts, and modern reinforcement learning approaches like those tested in Los Angeles and Pittsburgh have shown marginal improvements at best.

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis is already falsified by real-world evidence where adaptive signal systems using similar optimization techniques have repeatedly failed to handle sudden traffic pattern changes or unusual events.
failure_modes.evidence: Numerous deployments of adaptive traffic systems have collapsed during incidents like accidents, special events, or weather disruptions, exactly when the gradient descent mechanism would be most needed but least effective.

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis targets a solution to a problem that has already been solved more effectively through different approaches, making the entire enterprise scientifically questionable.
failure_modes.evidence: Modern traffic signal optimization using centralized AI systems with predictive capabilities has already demonstrated superior performance to local adaptive approaches, rendering this gradient descent approach obsolete before implementation.
